questions.q: Why is sending a photo base64-encoded inside a JSON body a poor choice?
questions.explain: Every 3 bytes become 4 characters, and a JSON parser needs the complete text. Multipart sends raw bytes that can be streamed to disk piece by piece.
options: Base64 makes the body about a third larger, and JSON must be held in memory whole before it can be parsed
Base64 is a form of encryption that slows the server down

questions.q: In a multipart/form-data body, what is the boundary?
questions.explain: The client picks a string that does not appear in the data. Each part starts after --BOUNDARY, and the body ends with --BOUNDARY--.
options: The maximum size of the upload
A random string, announced in the Content-Type header, that separates the parts
The first bytes of the file
The name of the form field

questions.q: Node.js can parse multipart with await request.formData(). Why does the lesson write a streaming parser instead?
questions.explain: For small forms, formData() is fine. For uploads of many megabytes from many users at once, only a streaming parser keeps memory flat. Production code uses a library such as busboy for this.
options: formData() reads the whole body into memory first, which is what uploads must avoid
It is faster to parse by hand

questions.q: Why does the parser keep back the last delimiter.length - 1 bytes of each chunk when it has not found a delimiter?
questions.explain: Network chunks can cut anywhere, including in the middle of \r\n--BOUNDARY. Holding back just less than a full delimiter means a split delimiter is always found once the next chunk arrives.
options: To make chunks equal in size
They might be the start of a delimiter that finishes in the next chunk; writing them out would put part of the boundary into the file
Because the last bytes of a chunk are always padding

questions.q: The parser awaits every sink.write. What does that achieve when the disk is slower than the network?
questions.explain: This is backpressure: the slowest step sets the pace. Without the await, chunks would pile up in memory while the disk catches up.
options: Nothing; it only makes the code look tidy
The parser stops pulling chunks from the request, so Node.js stops reading the socket and memory stays flat
The upload fails with a timeout
Chunks are written out of order

questions.q: A request says Content-Length: 5000. Why does the server still count the bytes it receives?
questions.explain: A declared length is useful to refuse obviously huge uploads early. The only reliable limit is the one enforced while the bytes stream in.
options: Because the header is in kilobytes
The header is written by the client; the body can be longer, and chunked uploads have no length at all
Because counting is needed for the checksum

questions.q: Which status code means "the upload is larger than the server accepts"?
questions.explain: 413 is for a body that is too big. 415 is for a type the server does not accept, such as HTML sent as a "photo".

questions.q: Why does the server decide a file's type from its first bytes instead of the part's Content-Type or the file extension?
questions.explain: An attacker names an HTML file photo.jpg and labels it image/jpeg. Its first bytes are still <html>, which is not a JPEG signature.
options: The header and the extension are labels the client chose; the magic number is in the data itself
Because sniffing is faster than reading a header
Because browsers do not send extensions

questions.q: A file starts with a valid JPEG signature. What does that not prove?
questions.explain: Sniffing checks the start only. A file can have a valid header and hostile data after it. Services that display images to many people often re-encode every upload in a background job, which keeps only real image data.
options: That the file claims to be a JPEG
That the rest of the file is a harmless, valid image
That the first three bytes are FF D8 FF
That the file is not a PNG

questions.q: Why is an upload stored under a random id instead of its filename?
questions.explain: The client's name is kept only as cleaned-up metadata for display. The storage key, and the extension (from the sniffed type), are chosen by the server.
options: The filename is client input: it can contain ../, collide with another file, or be very long; a random key avoids all of that
Filenames are not sent in multipart bodies
Operating systems forbid dots in filenames

questions.q: Why does the sink write to <id>.part and rename it at the end?
questions.explain: A rename within one file system is atomic: readers see either no file or the complete file. It also makes cleanup of interrupted uploads easy.
options: A half-written file is never visible under its final name, and a leftover .part file is clearly incomplete
Because the extension is not known until the end
To hide the file from the checksum

questions.q: What does the wx flag in createWriteStream(path, { flags: "wx" }) do?
questions.explain: It guarantees an upload never overwrites an existing file, even if two random ids ever collided or a bug reused one.
options: Opens the file for reading and writing
Creates the file for writing, and fails if a file with that name already exists
Writes the file with execute permission

questions.q: A request contains a valid photo, then an unexpected field that makes it fail. What should happen to the photo already written?
questions.explain: A rejected request must leave nothing behind, or the disk slowly fills with files nobody can find or delete. That is why abort also removes a finished file.
options: Delete it: the request failed as a whole, and an orphaned file would never be referenced
Move it to a quarantine folder forever

questions.q: What is the cleaned-up display name (passwd.jpg from ../../etc/passwd.jpg) used for?
questions.explain: It keeps the seller's friendly name without letting it touch the file system. Even cleaned, it is still client input, so it is never used to build a path.
options: Only for showing people, for example in a list or a download header

questions.q: What makes a signed URL impossible to forge?
questions.explain: Anyone can read the path and the expiry in the URL. Without the secret, nobody can compute a matching signature for a changed path or a later expiry.
options: The URL is long and hard to guess
It carries an HMAC of the path and the expiry, made with a secret only the server knows

questions.q: Why must the expiry time be inside the signed data, not just added to the URL?
questions.explain: Everything that limits a permission (path, method, expiry) must be signed. Unsigned parts of the URL are just suggestions.
options: Otherwise anyone could change expires to a later time and the signature would still match
Because browsers cache URLs with dates

questions.q: Why does checkSignedUrl compare signatures with timingSafeEqual instead of ===?
questions.explain: A comparison whose time does not depend on where the inputs differ gives an attacker nothing to measure.
options: === stops at the first different character, and the time difference can leak the signature piece by piece

questions.q: A signed download link leaked. How can you stop it working before it expires?
questions.explain: A signed URL is valid as long as its signature checks out. Changing the secret invalidates every link; a per-file version invalidates just one. Short lifetimes limit the damage in the first place.
options: Rotate the signing secret, or include a per-file version in what is signed and change it

questions.q: What does the response header X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff tell the browser?
questions.explain: Browsers used to "sniff" and could decide that an "image" was really HTML and run it. nosniff turns that off, so the server's (sniffed and trusted) type is the only one.
options: To use the declared Content-Type and not guess a different type from the content
To download the file instead of showing it
That the file was scanned for viruses

questions.q: Why serve uploaded PDFs with Content-Disposition: attachment?
questions.explain: Documents can contain scripts and links. Downloading them, and serving user content from a separate domain, keeps them away from your site's cookies and pages.
options: The browser saves the file instead of rendering it inside your site, where active content could run with your site's origin
It is required for all files over 1 MB

questions.q: Two servers behind a load balancer save uploads to their own local folders. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: Local disks are per machine. Object storage (S3, GCS, R2, MinIO) gives every server the same bucket, and it outlives any single server.
options: Nothing, as long as both folders exist
A file uploaded through one server is missing when a request lands on the other, and files are lost when a server is replaced

questions.q: With a presigned PUT URL, who sends the file's bytes to the bucket?
questions.explain: Your servers never carry the bytes, which saves bandwidth and memory. Afterwards, the client tells your API the upload is done, and a background job checks the object before it is published.
options: Your API server, after receiving them from the browser
The browser, directly; your API only checked the user and signed the URL

questions.q: Where should the record "seller 7 uploaded products/7/5f0c.jpg, 48,213 bytes, SHA-256 …, pending review" live?
questions.explain: Metadata is what you query, join, authorise and delete by. Keeping it in the database, pointing at the object's key, lets you find every file of a product or user, for example to erase it.
options: In your database, while the bytes live in object storage

questions.q: Why do many services re-encode uploaded photos before publishing them?
questions.explain: It is slow and can crash on hostile files, so it runs in a background job while the upload stays pending.
options: Re-encoding keeps only image data: it removes hidden payloads and EXIF metadata such as the GPS position where the photo was taken
To make every photo a PNG

questions.q: The parser reads a part's headers. What does this print?
questions.explain: The parser reports exactly what the client wrote, including a path in the filename and a content type that does not match the extension. Deciding what to trust is the next step's job.

questions.q: Two chunks arrive, and the delimiter is split between them. What does this print?
questions.explain: The delimiter is 7 bytes, so the parser holds back the last 6 bytes of the first chunk (DEF\r\n-), which might be the start of a delimiter, and writes only ABC. With the second chunk the full delimiter appears, and the rest of the data, DEF, is written. The file is exactly ABCDEF, with no piece of the boundary in it.

questions.q: A sink with a 10-byte limit receives three chunks. What does this print?
questions.explain: Exactly 10 bytes is allowed; the third chunk pushes the total past the limit, and the upload stops right there, without reading the rest of the body.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: %PDF is 25 50 44 46. The SVG (which can contain scripts) matches nothing on the allow-list. The two-byte input is too short to match the four-byte PNG signature: missing bytes are undefined, which equals no byte.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both kinds of path separator are split away, leading dots are removed (no hidden files), and characters such as quotes, which could break a Content-Disposition header, become underscores. A missing name gets a default.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The same inputs always give the same signature; a different path or expiry gives a different one. A SHA-256 HMAC is 32 bytes, which is 43 characters in base64url without padding.

questions.q: A link expires at 1,000 seconds. What does this print?
questions.explain: The link is valid strictly before its expiry time. At the expiry second itself it is already refused.
questions.code:
const check = (now: number, expires: number) => (now < expires ? "ok" : "expired");
console.log([999, 1_000, 1_001].map((now) => check(now, 1_000)));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Base64 turns every 3 bytes into 4 characters, so 3 MB becomes 4 MB of text, before JSON escaping and parsing make it worse.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With wx, creating a file that already exists fails with EEXIST instead of silently replacing it. An upload can never overwrite another file by accident.

questions.q: Two sellers upload the same photo under different names. What does this print?
questions.explain: A checksum depends only on the bytes, not on names or who uploaded them, so identical files have identical hashes and any change gives a new one. SHA-256 is 32 bytes, 64 hex characters. Stored with the metadata, it detects corruption and duplicates.

questions.q: Write boundaryFrom(contentType): return the boundary from multipart/form-data; boundary=… (1 to 70 characters, optionally in quotes), or throw Error("not multipart").
questions.explain: The boundary comes from a header the client wrote, so it is checked: the right media type, a sane length, and the quoted form handled. Anything else is a 400.
questions.expected:
----abc123
x y
not multipart
not multipart

questions.q: Write isPng(bytes): true only when the first 8 bytes are 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A.
questions.explain: Every signature byte must match. A text that merely contains "PNG" fails at the first byte, and a truncated header fails because the missing bytes are undefined.

questions.q: Finish makeCounter(limit): its add(chunk) adds the chunk's length and throws Error("413: over LIMIT bytes") as soon as the total passes the limit.
questions.explain: The limit is checked on every chunk, so the upload stops the moment it becomes too big, whatever the request's headers claimed.

questions.q: Write displayName(filename): keep only the last path segment (split on / and \), replace anything other than letters, digits, _, ., - and space with _, remove leading dots, and use "upload" if nothing is left.
questions.explain: The result is safe to show and to put in a header. It is still never used as a storage path: the stored file is named by a random key.

questions.q: Write isValid(path, expires, sig, now) using the provided sign function: the signature must match sign(path, expires) and now must be before expires.
questions.explain: Changing the path or the expiry breaks the signature, and an expired link is refused. The toy sign here only shows the shape: a real server uses an HMAC with a random secret (createHmac) and compares with timingSafeEqual.

questions.q: Write storageKey(productId, id, type) that builds an object key like products/7/5f0c.jpg, taking the extension from the sniffed type (never from the client's filename).
questions.explain: The key is built only from values the server controls: the product id it authorised, a random id, and the sniffed type. The client's name, even a misleading rice.png for a JPEG, does not appear.
